utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start, I've got no transcript on my screen. It's okay now. It's okay. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Case Number IT-03-72-I, the Prosecutor versus Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I have the appearances. Prosecution, first.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. For the Prosecution, from left to right, the case manager Lakshmie Walpita, the trial attorney Sabine Bauer, Alex Whiting, and Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours from left to right as well, the case manager, Mr. Danilo Cirkovic, my co-counsel, Mr. Robert Fogelnest, and I, myself, Peter Michael Mueller.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mueller. Mr. Babic, first of all, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I did not yet hear you in a language I understand because I was on the wrong channel. But I read that your answer was: "Yes, Your Honour." Yes, thank you, Mr. Babic. We are here today to hear an amended joint motion for consideration of a plea agreement between Milan Babic and the Office of the Prosecutor pursuant to Rule 62 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. This amended motion was filed on the 22nd of January, and it was preceded by another motion filed on the 12th of January which was also a motion to consider a plea agreement between Milan Babic and the Office of the Prosecutor. Therefore, it needs some explanation what has been changed. The previous motion -- in the previous motion, Mr. Babic committed himself to enter a guilty plea, a plea in which he would plead guilty to aiding and abetting a joint criminal enterprise in respect of count 1; that is, a joint criminal enterprise that committed the crime of persecution. Attached to that first motion was a statement of facts. The Chamber has read that statement of facts and has read the plea agreement, and the Chamber at that time had some doubts as to whether the legal qualification attached to these facts was appropriate. Therefore, the question was whether it was proper to qualify these facts as aiding and abetting to the joint criminal enterprise. Since the Chamber was of a provisional view that this legal qualification might be inconsistent with the facts, the Chamber has sent a message through the senior legal officer to inform the parties about this doubt. This has caused the parties to enter a new plea agreement, and it's this new plea agreement that we will consider today. First of all, I'd like to go in brief through the plea agreement. The accused, so you, Mr. Babic, you committed yourself, you agreed, to plead guilty to count 1 of the indictment alleging persecutions, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(h) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. You also agreed, as we read in paragraph 3 of the plea agreement, that you're pleading guilty to count 1 because you're, in fact, guilty as a coperpetrator of the joint criminal enterprise, that is, you acknowledge full responsibility for your actions that are the subject of the indictment. The Prosecution has committed itself according to paragraph 4 of the plea agreement that the Prosecution would move to dismiss without prejudice to either party the remaining charges against Milan Babic as set out in the indictment at the time of the acceptance of a guilty plea by the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution committed itself further to recommend to the Trial Chamber that it impose a term of imprisonment of no more than 11 years, and the agreement says that you, Mr. Babic, that you understand that the Trial Chamber is not bound to accept any recommendation and that the Trial Chamber may impose a sentence above or below the recommendation of the Prosecution. It's also stated that the Defence may recommend any sentence it deems appropriate. Further, the Prosecution has committed itself to certain measures of protection and safety. The factual basis of the plea agreement is set out in an annex to it. May I perhaps at this moment ask you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, if the indictment will be amended upon the acceptance of a guilty plea on count 1, what exactly would be amended? Would it just be striking out the counts 2 up to 5 as we find them on page 6 of the English version of the indictment? Or would there be any other changes in the previous parts of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there would be additional changes in the section "individual criminal responsibility." And also in the -- in count 1, wherever there is a reference to the mode of liability of Mr. Babic, we would make a change. We would actually precisely then only plea coperpetration committing in the form of a coperpetrator in a JCE. So we would drop aiding and abetting. We would drop the other modes of liability that are claimed here in the alternative in the paragraphs 4 through to 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To be also even more precise, we think that Mr. Babic's intent reflects more the JCE 3 type of participation, we would also slightly modify paragraph 9 where this issue is addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that means that also on the parts of the indictment on which the accused would plead guilty, that amendments still have to be made. I mean, I was in the -- it was the understanding of the Chamber that you would take out the remaining parts, but I do understand that changes are needed as well in respect of the part of the indictment on which the accused committed himself to plead guilty.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But Your Honours, as those forms of liability are all pleaded in the alternative, the plea agreement actually makes a clear distinction what is the plea about. We do not think that we would need to amend the indictment when the plea agreement is sufficiently clear that Mr. Babic pleads to coperpetration, which automatically shows that the other parts of the indictment would not be valid any more. The other modes of liability. If it were -- because it's alternatively charged, we felt that we would not need to make these amendments because of the plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the mode of liability, nothing else would change as far as facts are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's just the mode of liability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the understanding of the Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the understanding of the Defence as well, very clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mueller. Then we come to the next part of the plea agreement, and that is the factual basis. The factual basis of the plea agreement lists first of all the positions that Mr. Babic held during a longer period of time, that he was a member of the League of Communists of Croatia, that he was a delegate to the last congress of the League of Communists. That's all introductory remarks, so that's about I would say his political past, more or less, which is not the most relevant part of the statement of facts, that he held a senior position in the SDS municipal committee in Knin, and that he assumed the position of president of the SDS party from 1992, and that he held that position until 1995. From 1990 to 1994, he held the position of president of the municipal assembly in Knin, and he later was the president of the Serbian National Council. From December 1990, he was president of the temporary executive council of the Serbian Autonomous District Krajina, and on the 30th of April, he was elected president of the executive council of the SAO Krajina. Later, on the 29th of May 1991, he became the president of the government of the SAO Krajina. On the 1st of August of that same year, he signed a decision applying the law on defence of the Republic of Serbia to the territory of the SAO Krajina, and this made him de jure commander of all armed forces of the SAO Krajina, including special-purpose units of the Krajina Ministry, and commander of the Territorial Defence forces of the SAO Krajina. I'm saying de jure because it's also stated in the statement of facts that he had not at all times de facto control over these units. When the SAO Krajina proclaimed itself the Republic of Serbian Krajina on the 19th of December 1991, Mr. Babic was appointed president. And you held this position until 159th of February 1992, Mr. Babic. Later, a few years later, in April 1994, Mr. Babic became the minister of foreign affairs of the RSK government, but that is beyond the time scope of the indictment. But just to give some of the background. Just to summarise, and the Defence or the Prosecution would certainly correct me if my summary is not a correct one, Mr. Babic was very much concerned about the position of the Serb Croats in the area I just mentioned, and for that reason he was involved in the formation of the association of Serbian municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika. In 1990, he became president of that association. The purpose of it was to introduce Serbian regional autonomy in Croatia. This assembly in July 1990 passed a declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serbian nations in Croatia. The Serbian National Council was established as the executive body of this assembly. This Serbian National Council met for the first time in July 1990 in Knin. In August 1990, Milan Babic contacted Slobodan Milosevic to complain about the treatment of Serbs in the area around Knin, and Milosevic directed Milan Babic to meet with the president of the SFRY, Mr. Borisav Jovic, and such a meeting took place on the 13th of August 1990. Originally, Milan Babic viewed President Milosevic as the leader and the protector of all the ethnic Serbs in Yugoslavia. Milan Babic sought the assistance of Milosevic in protecting the Serb population in Krajina, and he was assured by Milosevic that they would be protected by the JNA. But the trust which Milan Babic had placed in Milosevic was undermined in March 1991 because it turned out that the objectives of Milosevic were not exactly the same as the ones Mr. Babic had in mind. On from that moment, from August 1990, a parallel structure, as it is called in the indictment, started emerging in the Krajina. It comprised members of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and the State Security Service of Serbia, the SDS in Croatia, and policemen in the Serbian municipalities in Croatia which ultimately answered directly and exclusively to Slobodan Milosevic. The statement of facts states that Milan Babic was not a member of this parallel structure and had no ability to control their actions. Milan Babic was aware of this parallel structure and shared its goal of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. creating a state for all Serbs. And although he had different views on the methods and means to obtain the goal of a Serbian state, he provided support to the parallel structure's aim of achieving a state for all Serbs through conflict and force by fail -- through conflict and force. And he did so by failing to publicly speak out against their methods, and by continuing to exercise the duties of his office in participating in the arming of Serbs in Croatia, creating and staffing political and military structures for a separate Serb entity in Croatia, and obtaining finance for these military structures. As far as my reading was not very clear, I emphasise that the support to the parallel structure's aim of achieving a state for all Serbs through conflict and force, this support was provided by failing to publicly speak out against these methods. In December 1990, under the leadership of Milan Babic, the association of municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika became the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina. Milan Babic was the leader of this SAO Krajina, and in April 1991, he was formally appointed president of the executive council. In May 1991, he became the prime minister of the SAO Krajina. Following a nomination by a majority of the temporary executive council of the SAO Krajina, Milan Babic appointed, on the 4th of January 1991, Milan Martic to be secretary for internal affairs of the SAO Krajina. Mr. Babic was aware that Mr. Martic was a key figure in the parallel structure. In a later stage, in -- let me first mention that in paragraph 20, the statement of facts says that the government of the SAO Krajina never had any effective control over Martic and the police force in Krajina, and that attempts to remove him were unsuccessful due to the support that Mr. Martic received from Mr. Milosevic and other members of the parallel structure. In March 1991, Babic asked Milosevic what was going on. He was told not to worry and to return to Knin. He was then informed about weapons already being bought, and he was later shown that these weapons had arrived. Milan Babic sought the assistance of Mr. Milosevic in getting professional training for the Krajina police. In March 1991, Mr. Babic endorsed, in his capacity as president of the Knin Municipal Assembly, a decision of the Assembly to completely and permanently separate the Knin Municipality from the Republic of Croatia. Then the statement of facts contains some disagreement on what exactly should be done at that moment, whether the SAO Krajina should join the Republic of Serbia, or rather the -- to join the other Yugoslavian entities at that time in existence. In May 1991, the SAO Krajina Assembly appointed Mr. Milan Martic minister of defence of the SAO Krajina, so it was not Mr. Babic who appointed him but it was with his acquiescence. Mr. Babic was aware that the forces under the command of Milan Martic were engaged in attacks of Croat civilians. The Assembly reappointed Mr. Martic as minister of the interior of the SAO Krajina in June 1991. Since no one was immediately appointed to replace Martic as minister of defence, for a period of time Milan Babic assumed that role. In the beginning of July 1991, we are now coming close to the period covered by the indictment, Mr. Babic signed orders as minister of defence of the SAO Krajina creating TO formations, Territorial Defence formations, within the SAO Krajina and appointing commanders to these formations. Milan Babic issued an order mobilising all staffs and units of the Territorial Defence in the SAO Krajina and as noted previously, on the 1st of August 1991, that's the first day covered by the indictment, Milan Babic issued a decision applying the law on defence of the Republic of Serbia to the SAO Krajina and making himself the commander of the armed forces of the SAO Krajina, including all special-purpose units of the SAO Krajina and of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina. Mr. Babic performed the duties connected with his position. And on the 8th of August, Milan Babic appointed Mile Martic under pressure from Milosevic to be deputy commander of the SAO Krajina Territorial Defence. Mr. Babic also signed orders creating TO formations, Territorial Defence formations, and appointing Territorial Defence commanders throughout the territory. After a short description of what happened in -- on from September 1991, the statement of facts continue that Milan Babic became aware -- where he was already aware of the plans of the other joint criminal enterprise members regarding the forcible removal of the Bosnian Muslims, but at least that from August 1991 following the attack on Kijevo, Mr. Babic became aware that the JNA and the parallel structure were not protecting the Serbs in Croatia, but were, along with local Serb Territorial Defence forces in the Krajina and with Martic's police, engaged in a war for territory to create the western borders of a new Serbian state. He saw that the creation of a Serbian state would include the forcible, permanent removal of the non-Serb populations from Serb-dominated areas of Croatia through a discriminatory campaign of persecution. And this war, to create a Serbian state, was the basis of the joint criminal enterprise described in the indictment whose purpose was the permanent, forcible removal of the majority of Croats and other non-Serb population from approximately one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia in order to make it part of the new Serb-dominated state. Mr. Babic became aware that this Serbian state was being created and maintained through the ethnic resettlement of the Croat and other non-Serb population within the Serb-dominated areas of Croatia. And although he had different views on the appropriate methods and means to obtain the goal of a Serbian state, he continued to cooperate and support those who sought to execute this plan with violent means. From August 1991, Milan Babic was aware of the intent of the members of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly resettle the Croatian and other non-Serb populations within the targeted areas. While he favoured a peaceful solution to the crisis, he knowingly and intentionally participated in the common design involving the perpetration of the crimes of persecutions as he, according to the statement of facts, himself put it, he became an ethnic egoist, a person who exclusively wanted to see the interests of people to which he belonged while he neglected the interests and suffering of the other peoples, at the time, the Croatian people. The statement of facts then continues stating persons who participated in the joint criminal enterprise including Slobodan Milosevic, Milan Martic, Goran Hadzic, Jovica Stanisic, Vojislav Seselj, and Ratko Mladic. This is not a complete enumeration, but I mentioned a few of them. In paragraph 33 of the statement of facts, it's set out in more detail in what ways Mr. Babic participated in this joint criminal enterprise. First, in his capacity as the president of the SNC and later as president and prime minister of the SAO Krajina in the area of RSK, he formulated, he promoted, he participated in and encouraged the development and implementation of the SDS and SAO Krajina RSK government policies which advanced the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. He was instrumental in the establishment, the support, and the maintenance of government bodies ruling the SAO Krajina which, in cooperation with the JNA and the parallel power structure, implemented the objectives of the joint criminal enterprise and participated in the commission of crimes listed in the indictment. As already said before, he was also de jure commander of the Territorial Defence forces. And although he did not endorse Mile Martic's methods and criminality, and also did not share his state of mind with respect to ethnic cleansing, Mr. Babic nevertheless cooperated with Milan Martic which led to Martic's command and control over what is called the Martic police involved in the commission of crimes. When in the summer of 1991 Milan Babic tried to get control over Martic's police, he had no success in doing so. He also participated in the provision of financial, materiel, logistical, and political support necessary for the military takeover of the territories in the SAO Krajina, which resulted in the subsequent forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population by the Territorial Defence forces, which acted in cooperation with the JNA and with Martic's police. He made ethnically-based inflammatory speeches during public events and in the media that added to the atmosphere of fear and hatred among Serbs living in Croatia, and as such, helped form the opinion of the public that Serbs could only be safe in a state of their own. He requested the assistance of, or he facilitated the participation of JNA forces to establish and maintain the SAO Krajina furthering the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. And he encouraged and assisted in the acquisition of arms and the distribution to Croatian Serbs to further the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. What, then, happened is described in more detail, the campaign of persecutions in the paragraphs 13 to 15 of the indictment. While Mr. Babic was aware that crimes such as imprisonment mentioned in 15(b), deportation and forcible transfer as we find it in paragraph 15(c) of the indictment, and the destruction of property, 15(d), as described in the indictment were being committed in the targeted territories, he did not know the details and the scale of the events that were occurring in the villages throughout the targeted areas at the time. However, he knew from what he observed that the crimes listed in the indictment were the likely outcome of the pursuit of the objective of the joint criminal enterprise and the campaign of persecutions. At the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, in relation to the imprisonment, he took steps to alleviate the problems by appointing provisional prison staff. With respect to the murders charged in paragraph 15(a) of the indictment, Milan Babic did not know they were occurring at the time, but knew from what he observed that such killings were the likely outcome of the pursuit of the objective of the joint criminal enterprise and the campaign of persecutions. This is, although in some respects summarised and some respects literally, the content of the statement of facts underlying the plea agreement, would any of the parties have any additions to make or corrections to make as to this summary?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Having gone through the factual basis of the agreement, I'll just briefly mention a few other elements of the plea agreement. Mr. Babic agrees to cooperate fully with the Office of the Prosecution and has cooperated already. He agrees to testify in other cases and to meet with the Prosecution. He also committed himself to the truthfulness of whatever information and testimony he will provide. Mr. Babic, the plea agreement also says that you understand that the maximum sentence that can be imposed by a Trial Chamber for a guilty plea to the charge of persecutions is a term of imprisonment up to and including the remainder of your life. You also understand that pursuant to Rule 62 ter (B), the Trial Chamber, as already indicated before, is not bound by any agreement between you and the Office of the Prosecution. You Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. also committed yourself to not withdrawing your guilty plea to or appeal your conviction pursuant to this guilty plea. But you reserved your right to appeal against sentence imposed if it comes to that. The plea agreement, I further say, is what will guide the Chamber in imposing sentence, and you have a full understanding of that. You also understand that the parties will provide information to the Chamber in respect of sentencing. You waived, you gave up some rights as well. First of all, the right to plead not guilty, which hardly needs to be said if you committed yourself to plead guilty because you can't do both of them. Of course, it influences your position, that would be different at trial, where you would have the facility to prepare and put forward your defence; that you would be tried without undue delay in your presence; that you would have the right to examine witnesses or have them examined; that, of course, you waived the right not to be compelled to testify against yourself because you, in pleading guilty, you admit your guilt; and that you gave up the right of appeal. Finally, the plea agreement says that you voluntarily entered into this agreement, and therefore if you would plead guilty, that it would be a voluntary plea; that no threats were made to you to induce you to enter this guilty plea; and that no other promises have been given to you apart from the ones mentioned in the plea agreement. You have signed this plea agreement. May I ask you whether you fully understood what your commitments are? It has been confirmed already by your signature and by Defence counsel, but the Chamber would like to hear from yourself as well whether you are fully aware of what you signed to and what the consequences may be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're also aware of what moved the parties to enter into this new plea agreement and what the difference is between aiding and abetting, and that the Chamber had, as a provisional view, that in the earlier plea agreement there was some inconsistency as to the legal qualification of the facts mentioned in the statement of facts in qualifying this as aiding and abetting to the joint criminal enterprise rather than as participation in a joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that this was further explained to you by counsel, and that you understood their explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Having gone in some detail through the plea agreement, I would first like to ask any of the Judges would have any questions in respect of the plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge El Mahdi has a question for -- I do not know which of the parties. Perhaps both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have a question for the Prosecution regarding the contents of paragraph 33(d) and paragraph 34. I have to admit that I have a problem in comparing two paragraphs. I will quote paragraph 33(d) for you. [In English] "methods and criminality, nor did he share his state of mind with respect to ethnic cleansing, Milan Babic nevertheless cooperated with Milan Martic." [Interpretation] Up until the last sentence which says as follows: [In English] "And the parallel structure without success, and thereafter he continued to cooperate with them." [Interpretation] My question is the following: Does it not indicate a common intent between Mr. Babic and members of the joint criminal enterprise, among other things, and in particular, Mr. Martic? To be precise, I do not see a cooperation without a common intent.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution made a clear distinction between various members of the JCE in this document and throughout the proceedings in this case and other related cases. What we say clearly in paragraph 30 is that Mr. Babic knowingly and intentionally participated in the common design involving the perpetration of the crime of persecution, but the intent of Mr. -- or rather, the methods of Milan Martic were quite different from what Mr. Babic shared and endorsed because it goes further than other members of the JCE went, because Mr. Milan Martic not only wanted to forcibly remove the majority of the Croat population and non-Serb population in those territories; he went much further than that because what he was engaged in was a persecution campaign, including the murders and the really extensive destruction and the extensive mistreatment of detainees and the extensive forcible removal of the population that Mr. Babic did not even know the exact details of, as you can see in paragraph 34. We clearly wanted to make a distinction between the state of mind of Mr. Martic and the state of mind of Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But can you further elaborate, what was the exact intent of Mr. Babic? Did he have, yes or no, the intent to commit persecutions?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he did. He did from August 1991 onwards, when he saw what was going on and he continued to participate with other members of the JCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This position, is it shared by the Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's shared with the Defence. It can't be expressed any clearer as by the representative of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few questions as well. May I draw to your attention paragraph 34 of the statement of facts. On the end, on the bottom of page 13, English version, it says: "With respect to the murders charged in paragraph 15(a) of the indictment, Milan Babic did not know they were occurring at the time. But knew from what he observed that such killings were the likely outcome of the pursuit of the objective of the joint criminal enterprise in the campaign of persecutions." I do understand this to be a reference in legally technical terms to what I would call the type 3 joint criminal enterprise where other members of the joint criminal enterprise commit acts even beyond what was the shared design. But I have a more factual question. It reads: "Milan Babic did not know" -- these were the murders -- "they were occurring at the time." How does the Chamber have to understand this? That, for example, if a murder or murders were committed in October 1991, that Mr. Babic did not know at that moment, well, let's say on that day, that these murders were committed? Or does it also mean that Mr. Babic would not know about these murders even in early November or mid-November when perhaps other murders were committed which he was not aware of, of them being committed at that time, but knowing that murders had been, for example, committed in October?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: It's the latter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he later on -- let me just... So he never heard, he never knew about any of the murders listed in 15(a) which are considerable numbers of people killed in at least not individual incidents. I see in 15(a), I see the killing of 56 people on the 21st of October 1991; other 30 civilians, 24 civilians. I see 7 civilians killed in Lipovaca on the 28th of October. I see 10 civilians killed in the hamlet of Vukovici near Poljanak; 29 civilians killed in the village of Saborsko on the 12th of November. On the 18th of November, 38 non-Serb civilians killed in Skabrnja. Do I have to understand that Mr. Babic, during the indictment period, got no knowledge of these killings, or that he did not have knowledge of these killings while they were committed but perhaps may have obtained knowledge of them at a later stage, let's say one week after that or a month after that? I try to understand what exactly means "at the time."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Babic in his extensive interviews was asked, always mentioned that he learned about the details of these murders as you have referred to years later, not at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, details.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But that they occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That they occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So Mr. Babic was not aware of any killings occurring in the campaign of forcible removal of non-Serb -- non-Serb members of these villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would make a distinction between killings and murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Of course, when there is a war ongoing and when these attacks occur on the population, he of course knew about people dying in these villages, or in the territory. But he was not aware of the murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As described here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean by killing including civilians that were killed during the attacks, or when you're referring to killings are you only referring to, I would say, combatants or...?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To both. So I properly understand that Mr. Babic was aware of civilians killed during these attacks just as combatants were killed, not knowing, however, on murders, and I do understand that when speaking about murder you refer then to, I would say, these executions, more or less, of numbers of people driven together, and that he only learned about that at a later stage, at least not within the time covered by the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is my understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I seek confirmation from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Yes, this is also the understanding, Your Honours, as the Defence look at it. What we learned from our information from the client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any other source apart from the statement of Mr. Babic given during his interviews of the absence of his knowledge, and is there any source that would support a more general knowledge, for example, by newspapers or television reports on the occurrence of these murders?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, not that we are aware of. Of course, we put this to Mr. Babic, that from the media he would have knowledge in general terms of the matter. But as far as I recall, he said he was not in a position to receive this neutral media at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has there been any investigation as to whether only the, what you call, neutral media, although I have become aware in this Tribunal that it's not easy to find neutral media, whether any local media paid attention to it, whether any local newspapers paid attention to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we, of course, found is that the Croatian media reported about these events. At the same time the Serbian media reported the absolute contrary to what the Croats were reporting, and we could not establish whether Mr. Babic received such information. And we also could not establish that Mr. Babic read, for instance, international media at the time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything to add to this on the side of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: A little fact: When I remember correctly, Mr. Babic stated in the course of his interviews, and please correct me if I'm wrong, that at that time it was impossible to receive other TV programmes than the Serb ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They could even not receive Croatian television?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: No. That's what I understood. In that area he was living.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answers in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I offer an additional piece of information to the Court. I would invite the Trial Chamber's attention to, I believe it's de la Brosse's report. The Prosecutor commissioned a report to be done by a professor in Rheims which explains the propaganda campaign that was being conducted by both Belgrade in large part and Croatia. So it was very difficult for anyone to evaluate what the truth was under any circumstances. I think the Court would find that quite enlightening if you've not already had an opportunity to review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would the parties be willing to provide this to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have this report. It was filed in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it could be a joint filing by the parties. I have one other question about the inflammatory speeches. Are texts available of these speeches?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the Chamber receive copies of two extremes; that is, one in which Mr. Babic used the, I would say, the strongest language, and another one where he was mildest.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we will look for it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the parties could agree upon what was the strongest one and what was the mildest one. If you have any doubt, you could also provide one or two others so as to make it for the Chamber to decide what was the strongest one. So we want to -- we would like to see the both extremes of these speeches.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this moment in relation to the statement of facts, neither do I have any further questions in relation to the plea agreement as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have come to a point where I'd would like to invite the accused to plead. And from the plea agreement, I understand that perhaps we should limit the invitation to plead to count 1. Since there will be changes in the indictment anyhow, I think that we should -- I'd like to hear exactly from the Prosecution and Defence what will be the formulation of the count on which Mr. Babic intends to plead guilty. I mean, I don't think it's of great use to read all the rest of the indictment at this very moment since changes not yet known in detail will be made at a later stage. But I would like at least to know for sure what is the exact formulation of the count. As I read it up till this moment in the indictment, let me just take it, it is: "Persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(H) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal." And I do understand that the plea would then be that he pleads guilty to what I just read, adding "by coperpetratorship in a joint criminal enterprise." Is that a proper understanding of what the charge would be?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would be the charge. And actually, we did not now intend to amend the indictment. As I explained, it's pleaded in the alternative. And as long as he makes clear that he is now pleading guilty to coperpetration instead of aiding and abetting and the other forms as specified in paragraph 4 of the indictment and also paragraph 13, we wouldn't actually file an amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, yes. You would just ask leave to drop the remaining charges, the remaining four charges. So then I'll read, then, the -- yes, Mr. Mueller.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: As you may have already anticipated, Your Honour, I agree with that, and I agree to that addition to the count 1 in the sense you have quoted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Babic, may I invite you to stand. I'll read the first count of the indictment brought against you dated the 6th of November 2003. Persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(H), and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal, by participating as a coperpetrator in a joint criminal enterprise. How do you plead to this charge?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Please be seated. The Trial Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 1. Mr. Mueller.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would kindly ask you for permission that my client would make an additional short statement. Would you accept that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I would first like to continue the requirements of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: As you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand that he would like the opportunity at a later stage to make a short statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the first thing this Chamber will have to do is to satisfy itself that you have made this plea voluntarily and that no threats or no coercion was exercised. That was also the reason why I went with you through the plea agreement in this respect. The second thing this Chamber has to do to satisfy itself that this plea was informed; that's why we put questions to you specifically on the issue which made the party change the earlier agreement into the new one. The Chamber also has to consider -- to satisfy itself that the plea was not equivocal. And finally, the Chamber has to satisfy itself that a sufficient factual basis for the crime and your participation, that it does exist. In that respect, I'd like to invite the parties to tell the Chamber whether in respect of these questions, these issues on which the Chamber will have to satisfy itself, whether there's any additional submission you'd like to make or to add any piece of evidence which would make it easier for the Chamber to establish that, or there is sufficient factual basis for the plea. Perhaps first I now ask the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: There are not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to add something. In the Milosevic indictment, we named Mr. Babic as a member of the JCE, sharing the intent of the other members of the JCE to forcibly remove the non-Serb population from targeted areas. In the contact with him, Mr. Babic, however, made a distinction between himself and the other members of the JCE, stressing that he was, first, not aware of the criminal objective and the means to achieve this objective of the JCE, but only saw what was going on and from what he saw concluded and understood what the objective was. So that is from August 1991. He's not one of those who actually came up with the plan. And he also made clear that he was not in control of the forces conducting the persecution campaign, and the Prosecution found both of his statements correct because we, of course, have investigated the members of the JCE. We have a huge amount of information, and a huge amount of statements and documents that actually confirm this. So his claim is supported. And what you find in the factual basis is actually what we found on the basis on a huge amount of evidence that is not in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that. The Chamber will not take a decision today. The Chamber will consider whatever has been said here, and the Chamber will take a decision as soon as possible whether this plea is accepted or not and all the subsequent decisions that have to be taken, such as instructing the Registrar to set a day for sentence. Having recorded the plea and having heard the request of the Defence to give an opportunity to Mr. Babic to make a short statement...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I give an opportunity now to Mr. Babic to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I come before this Tribunal with a deep sense of shame and remorse. I have allowed myself to take part in the worst kind of persecution of people simply because they were Croats and not Serbs. Innocent people were persecuted; innocent people were evicted forcibly from their houses; and innocent people were killed. Even I learned what had happened, I kept silent. Even worse, I continued in my office, and I became personally responsible for the inhumane treatment of innocent people. The regret that I feel is the pain that I have to live for the rest of my life. These crimes and my participation therein can never be justified. I'm speechless when I have to express the depth of my remorse for what I have done and for the effect that my sins have had on the others. I can only hope that by expressing the truth, by admitting to my guilt, and expressing the remorse can serve as an example to those who still mistakenly believe that such inhumane acts can ever be justified. Only truth can give the opportunity for the Serbian people to relieve itself of its collective burden of guilt. Only an admission of guilt on my part makes it possible for me to take responsibility for all the wrongs that I have done. I hope that the remorse that I expressed will make it easier for the others to bear their pain and suffering. I have come to understand that enmity and division can never make it easier for us to live. I have come to understand that our -- the fact that we all belong to the same human race is more important than any differences, and I have come to understand that only through friendship and confidence we can live together in peace and friendship, and thus make it possible for our children to live in a better world. I have asked help from God to make it easier for me to repent, and I am thankful to God for making it possible for me to express my repentance. I ask from my brothers, Croats, to forgive us, their brother Serbs, and I pray for the Serb people to turn to the future and to achieve the kind of compassion that will make it possible to forgive the crimes. And lastly, I place myself at the full disposal of this Tribunal and international justice. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Is there anything any of the parties would like to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Mueller is nodding no. That's always a bit difficult to the transcript. So I expect he doesn't have anything to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am aware that there was some concern between the parties as far as preparing for a possible sentencing hearing is concerned, especially the time frame for presenting presentencing briefs. Since the Chamber has not yet accepted the plea, I find it inappropriate to discuss this at this very moment in this Court. But I invite the parties to bring to the attention of the senior legal officer whatever is in their minds and to discuss with him the matter, which is a very practical matter. Then we stay adjourned, and the Chamber will give a decision on the acceptance of the plea in due course.
